exercise_group.instructions: In Exercises 1–24, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) A negative entry $a_{ij}$ in a payoff matrix indicates the amount player $R$ has to pay player $C$ when $R$ choses action $i$ and $C$ choses action $j$.
(T/F) Every payoff matrix has at least one saddle point.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{x}$ is a vector whose entries sum to $1$, then $\mathbf{x}$ is a probability vector.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{x}$ is a pure strategy in a matrix game, then all the coordinates in $\mathbf{x}$ have the same value.
(T/F) Each strategy for player $R$ in a matrix game is a convex combination of the set of pure strategies for $R$.
(T/F) If $A$ is an $m \times n$ payoff matrix, then the strategy space for $R$ is the set of all probability vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.
(T/F) A strategy $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ for row player $R$ is optimal if the value of $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is equal to the value of the game to $R$.

(T/F) If $A$ is the payoff matrix for a matrix game, then the value of strategy $\mathbf{x}$ to player $R$, denoted $v(\textbf{x})$, is the minimum of the inner product of $\mathbf{x}$ with each of the columns of $A$.

(T/F) If $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ and $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ are optimal strategies for an $m \times n$ matrix game whose value is $v$, then $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is a convex combination of the pure strategies $\textbf{e}_{j}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ for which $E(\widehat{\textbf{x}},\textbf{e}_{j}) = v$.

(T/F) If $A$ is the payoff matrix for a $2 \times n$ matrix game, then the value of strategy $\textbf{x}(t)$ to player $R$, denoted $v(\textbf{x}(t))$, is the maximum value of $n$ linear functions of $t$.
(T/F) If a canonical linear programming problem has a feasible solution but no optimal solution, then the objective function must be unbounded on the feasible set.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{x}$ is an extreme point of the feasible set of a canonical linear programming problem, then $\mathbf{x}$ is an optimal solution.
(T/F) If the objective function in a canonical linear programming problem takes on arbitrarily large values in the feasible set, then the problem is infeasible.
(T/F) If a canonical linear programming problem is unbounded, then it must be feasible.
(T/F) If the feasible set of a canonical linear programming problem is unbounded, then the program has no optimal solution.
(T/F) The simplex method of solving a canonical linear programming problem begins by changing each constraint inequality into an equality.
(T/F) If $A$ is $m \times n$, then it will require $n$ slack variables to change $A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$ into a system of linear equations.
(T/F) In following the simplex method, when a variable goes “out” of a basic feasible solution, it stays out.
(T/F) In order to begin the standard simplex method, each term in the augmented column above the horizontal line must be a nonnegative number.
(T/F) When setting up the initial simplex tableau for a canonical linear programming problem, the coefficients of the objective function go in the bottom row.
(T/F) In setting up the dual linear programming problem, the matrix $A$ in the primal problem is replaced by $A^{- 1}$ in the dual problem.
(T/F) If a primal linear programming problem has an optimal solution, then its dual program is bounded.

(T/F) Let $P$ be a maximizing linear programming problem and let $P^{\ast}$ be its dual. If $P$ has an optimal solution, then the maximum value of the objective function of $P$ in its feasible set is equal to the minimum value of the objective function of $P^{\ast}$ in its feasible set.

(T/F) Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix game where all the entries in $A$ are positive. Let $\overset{ˉ}{\textbf{y}}$ and $\overset{ˉ}{\textbf{x}}$ be the optimal solutions to the related primal and dual linear programming problems, respectively, as defined in Section 9.4. If $\text{λ}$ is equal to the sum of the coordinates in $\overset{ˉ}{\textbf{x}}$, then the value of the matrix game is equal to $\text{λ}$.

Note that this has the same constraint inequalities as Exercise 25 (and hence the same feasible set), but the objective function is different.

Evaluate the objective function at each of the extreme points.

statement.paragraph: Try to use the simplex method to solve the problem in Exercise 27. Explain why it doesn’t work.

list.item: Set up the initial simplex tableau.
Try to apply the simplex method and explain why it does not work.
Graph the constraint inequalities and explain how they relate to your answer to part b.

statement.paragraph: The bottom row of the final tableau for a linear programming problem will have zeros as entries in the columns corresponding to the basic variables that are “in” the solution. There may also be zeros in some of the other columns in this bottom row. When this happens, the optimal solution will not be unique since these other variables could be brought into the solution without changing the value of the objective function.
